sources.name: GDP GROWTH
sources.label: Quarterly economic output, YoY
sources.description: Quarterly GDP growth, year-on-year. Rosstat confirmed full-year 2025 GDP growth of 1.0% — sharp deceleration vs. the defense-spending-led 4.3% peak in 2024. BOFIT and the Bank of Russia expect 2026 to print at a similar ~1% pace.
sources.whyItMatters: Headline GDP is now defense-spending-led; the civilian economy looks worse than the topline implies.

sources.name: INFLATION RATE
sources.label: Consumer Price Index, YoY
sources.description: Monthly headline CPI, year-on-year. After peaking at ~10.3% in Q1 2025, the Bank of Russia's 21% policy rate has dragged inflation back toward target. Real purchasing power continues to lag official inflation since wages have not kept up.
sources.whyItMatters: Wages have lagged official inflation since Q3 2022 — this is the best proxy for how a salary feels at the supermarket.

sources.name: RUBLE / USD
sources.label: Monthly close, ₽ per $1
sources.description: USD/RUB rate at month-close. Ruble strengthened sharply through late 2025 and 2026 to a three-year high near ₽75 as energy revenue stabilised, capital controls held, and the Bank of Russia kept policy rates elevated.
sources.whyItMatters: The ruble is the only daily-published indicator the Russian state can't easily massage — it's a real-time confidence vote.

sources.name: POLICY RATE
sources.label: Bank of Russia key rate, % p.a.
sources.description: Bank of Russia key policy rate. Cut for the seventh consecutive meeting in April 2026 to 14.50% as inflation eased. The rate path tracks the central bank's confidence — high rates mean the inflation fight isn't over and credit is being throttled.
sources.whyItMatters: The policy rate is the price of credit for households and firms — at 14.5% it's still painfully restrictive and a drag on the civilian economy.

sources.name: REAL WAGES
sources.label: Real wages YoY vs. CPI inflation
sources.description: Rosstat real-wage growth YoY (red) plotted against headline CPI YoY (navy). Defense-sector and labour-shortage wage premiums kept real wages running 5–9% above inflation through 2024–H1 2025; that wedge is now collapsing as the economy cools.
sources.whyItMatters: When real wages stop outrunning prices, the wartime social contract — high pay, low freedom — starts to wobble.

sources.name: SENTIMENT SCORE
sources.label: Public-search and news-tone proxy
sources.description: Indirect sentiment proxy from Google Trends queries on Russian-language hardship terms (relocation, prices, mobilisation). Scored 0–100 (100 = fully positive). Modest upward drift through 2025–26 reflects adaptation rather than improving conditions.
sources.whyItMatters: Public surveys are unreliable in autocracies; search behaviour is harder to fake.

sources.name: PUBLIC POLLS
sources.label: Independent life-satisfaction polling
sources.description: Levada Center's life-satisfaction composite (% reporting satisfied with life). Reading hit a 20-year high in late 2024 and has held in the mid-50s through 2025–26 — a counter-intuitive result driven by wartime adaptation and rising defense-sector wages.
sources.whyItMatters: Levada is the closest thing to independent polling left inside Russia — readers and policymakers cite it.

sources.name: EMIGRATION INDEX
sources.label: Monthly departures (thousands)
sources.description: Estimated monthly outflow combining Eurostat first-time asylum applications by Russian citizens with residency-permit data from Georgia and Armenia. Outflow has steadily declined from the 2022 mobilisation spike but remains an order of magnitude above pre-war baseline.
sources.whyItMatters: When educated workers leave faster than they're replaced, long-term economic capacity erodes regardless of headline numbers.

sources.name: NEWS NEGATIVITY
sources.label: Negative-tone share of Russia events
sources.description: Share of negative-tone Russia events on the GDELT 2.0 Goldstein scale, monthly average. Modest easing through 2025–26 as front-line activity stabilised, but still well above pre-war norms.
sources.whyItMatters: When state outlets emphasise fear and conflict, it tends to lead internal mobilisation or repression cycles.

sources.name: ROSSTAT GAP
sources.label: Official vs. independent estimate divergence
sources.description: Multiplier between Rosstat figures and independent estimates from BOFIT (Bank of Finland) and Yale CELI. Gap has narrowed as both BOFIT and Rosstat now estimate ~1% growth for 2025 — but the headline still overstates civilian-sector strength.
sources.whyItMatters: When official numbers diverge from independent estimates, the official narrative is harder to take at face value.

sources.name: ECON. FREEDOM
sources.label: Heritage Foundation index, 0–100
sources.description: Heritage Foundation Economic Freedom score. Russia's 2026 release printed 50.3 (−1.3 YoY), keeping it near the bottom of the global table. Annual cadence — only the latest two readings are shown to keep within the dashboard's 1-year scope.
sources.whyItMatters: Property rights and trade freedom are slow-moving structural metrics — they signal long-run trajectory, not month-to-month noise.

sources.name: PRESS FREEDOM
sources.label: RSF World Press Freedom Index, 0–100
sources.description: Reporters Without Borders World Press Freedom Index. Russia ranked 172/180 in the 2026 release; RSF flagged worldwide press freedom at a 25-year low. 48 journalists were detained as of April 2026. Annual cadence — last 2 readings shown.
sources.whyItMatters: Press freedom is the early-warning system for civilian conditions; when journalists are jailed, every other indicator becomes harder to verify.

sources.name: CORRUPTION INDEX
sources.label: Transparency Intl. CPI, 0–100
sources.description: Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index (latest published reading: 2025 release covers 2024 data). Russia scored 22/100, among the lowest globally, alongside Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. TI's Russian chapters operate in exile.
sources.whyItMatters: When state institutions are corrupt, headline economic numbers and welfare programmes have to be discounted heavily.

sources.name: DEFENSE BURDEN
sources.label: Military spending, % of GDP
sources.description: SIPRI estimate of Russian military expenditure as share of GDP. 2025 hit 7.5% (~$190bn, +5.9% YoY); the 2026 budget plans 6.3% (~14.9 trn roubles) as the Ministry of Defence economises. Still triple the global average of 2.5%.
sources.whyItMatters: Every rouble spent on defense is a rouble not spent on hospitals, schools, or pensions. The military burden is the most direct proxy for civilian-budget crowding-out.
